meta.subtitle: Rate-base growth is on plan and leverage is moderate for a utility, but upside beyond a year of consensus growth needs a re-rating, so we stay neutral

advisories: gate ceiling SELL (distress) — advisory, not applied

analystSentiment.commentary:
Atmos Energy's fiscal third quarter kept the regulated growth model on plan. Nine-month net income was $1,227.6 million, or $7.33 per diluted share, against $1,023.9 million, or $6.40, a year earlier, a {+ 20 percent +} increase. The August 5, 2026 earnings release reaffirmed fiscal 2026 guidance of $8.40 - $8.50 per diluted share.

The MD&A attributes most of that increase to positive rate outcomes driven by safety and reliability spending. It also credits $132.4 million of the nine-month result to Texas legislation on infrastructure spending; how much that benefit adds to growth from here is a question we take up in the growth section.

Net debt stood at $8.7B at FY25 year-end; on a trailing basis it is 3.7x EBITDA, with interest coverage of 12.8x. We read that as moderate leverage for a regulated utility, and the balance sheet section explains why the page's advisory distress flag does not change our view.

The shares have fallen from a 52-week high of $192.51 to $157.07, just above the $154.72 low, and no source on the page explains the move. Our Base case credits a year of consensus earnings growth at today's trailing multiple but does not assume the shares win back that lost ground, and on that anchor the expected upside is too thin for a BUY. We rate the shares **HOLD**.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Atmos Energy Corporation is a natural gas-only distributor headquartered in Dallas. It serves approximately 3.4 million residential, commercial, public authority, and industrial customers through six distribution divisions covering service areas in eight states, and it transports natural gas for others through its distribution and pipeline systems.

The company manages two reportable segments. Distribution covers regulated natural gas distribution and related sales; pipeline and storage is built mainly around the Atmos Pipeline-Texas division and natural gas transmission operations in Louisiana.

Earnings are set by regulators rather than by commodity prices, because gas costs pass through to customers without markup under purchased gas cost adjustment mechanisms. The investment case therefore turns on how much capital the company deploys and how quickly regulators let it earn a return on that capital.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body:
Atmos Energy is a rate-base compounder: it spends heavily on safety-driven modernization of its system and recovers much of that spending through mechanisms that shorten regulatory lag. The model is delivering, with diluted EPS higher in every year from FY21 to FY25 and a wider operating margin in FY25 than in FY21.

Against that, free cash flow is negative, so the plan depends on debt and equity markets, and our Base case earns only a year of consensus growth unless the shares re-rate. That leaves too little expected upside for the Bear-case risk, so we rate the shares **HOLD**.

catalysts: Decisions on the ratemaking requests still pending at June 30, 2026, which would add to annual operating income if granted.
Fiscal 2026 results against the EPS guidance, and any fiscal 2027 outlook the company provides.
Updates to the fiscal 2026 to 2030 capital plan, which sets the pace of rate-base growth.
risks: Regulators could disallow costs or modify the mechanisms that currently reduce regulatory lag.
Operations are concentrated in Texas, which also supplied this year's legislative earnings benefit.
Higher interest rates or tighter capital markets would raise the cost of funding a capital program that exceeds operating cash flow.
A pipeline accident could bring liability, fines and a loss of customer confidence beyond insurance limits.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended September 30.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue rose from $3.4B in FY21 to $4.7B in FY25, with FY25 up {+ +12.9% +}, but the line moves with gas costs passed through to customers, so operating income is the better gauge. Operating income grew from $0.9B to $1.6B over the same span, operating margin widened from 26.6% to 33.2%, and diluted EPS climbed from $5.12 to $7.46.

The quarter ended June 30, 2026 is the company's fiscal third quarter; the third-party financial series labels it Q2'26, and we use the company's naming. Revenue was $879.1M, {+ +4.8% +} year over year, at a 36.4% operating margin.

In the distribution segment, operating income rose {+ 14.3 percent +}. Rate adjustments, primarily in the Mid-Tex Division, added $21.0 million and residential customer growth and increased industrial load added $3.9 million, against a $20.0 million increase in depreciation expense and property taxes and a $9.4 million increase in employee-related costs. Texas infrastructure legislation lifted the segment's income before income taxes by $26.7 million in the quarter, including $17.8 million in operating expenses.

Read together, the listed operating drivers roughly offset each other: higher depreciation and property taxes absorbed most of the rate adjustments, and customer growth did not cover higher employee costs. Yet segment operating income still rose, so in our reading most of the rise sits outside the listed drivers, and the Texas infrastructure legislation is the one other item the MD&A names. That reading has a limit: the legislation became effective during the third quarter of fiscal 2025, the prior-year comparison quarter, so the 10-Q does not show how much of the operating-expense benefit is incremental, and part of the rise may still be underlying.

Throughput fell to 73,143 MMcf from 75,354 MMcf. The MD&A says the base customer charge only partially separates recovery from usage, so volume still matters, yet operating income rose despite the lower throughput.

On a trailing twelve-month basis, operating margin is 37.0% and net margin 28.5%.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended September 30.

financials.balanceCommentary:
Total debt rose from $7.3B in FY21 to $8.9B in FY25, while total equity grew faster, from $7.9B to $13.6B, so the capital program has been funded with a heavy equity component. The 10-Q puts equity capitalization at 59.8 percent at June 30, 2026; the earnings release rounds this to 60%, and we use the 10-Q figure. Debt dipped to $6.8B in FY23, the one year in the series with positive free cash flow, and has climbed since: net debt was $8.7B at FY25 year-end against $7.5B a year earlier.

On a trailing basis, net debt is 3.7x EBITDA and interest coverage is 12.8x. For a regulated utility that builds rate base with borrowed and equity capital by design, we read that as moderate leverage rather than strain. The point to watch is direction rather than level: net debt rises each year that capital spending outruns operating cash flow.

During the nine months ended June 30, 2026, the company completed approximately $2.2 billion of long-term debt and equity financing. Total liquidity was approximately $4.6 billion at quarter-end, made up of $521.0 million in cash and cash equivalents, $936.8 million available through equity forward sales agreements and $3,094.4 million in undrawn capacity under its credit facilities.

The page's fundamental gate reads DISTRESS and shows a SELL ceiling. The trigger is liquidity, not leverage: a current ratio below one (0.81 on a trailing basis, 0.77 at FY25 year-end), negative FY25 free cash flow (set out in the cash flow section), and FY25 year-end cash of $0.2B, which covers less than a year of that gap. The gate is advisory; it does not set or cap our label, which comes from the scenarios. We do not read it as a solvency signal here, because a regulated utility runs negative free cash flow while it builds rate base and the cash test leaves out the undrawn facilities and equity forwards above. What the flag does capture is real dependence on capital markets, which the cash flow section takes up.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended September 30.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Operating cash flow was $2.0B in FY25 against capital expenditure of $3.6B, leaving free cash flow of -$1.5B, an FCF margin of -32.2% and a trailing FCF yield of -7.6%. Free cash flow was negative in every year from FY21 to FY25 except FY23, when operating cash flow reached $3.5B. Dividends paid of $0.6B in FY25 come on top of that gap.

Spending is accelerating. Capital expenditures were $3,076.3 million in the nine months ended June 30, 2026, and the August 5, 2026 earnings release puts fiscal 2026 capital expenditure at approximately $4.2 billion. The MD&A says a significant portion of this investment is incurred under regulatory mechanisms that reduce lag to six months or less. In our view that shortens the wait before new spending earns a return, but it does not close the cash gap.

We do not expect free cash flow to turn positive while the fiscal 2026 to 2030 plan runs at its current scale, so debt and equity issuance must keep covering both capital spending and dividends. That makes continued access to debt and equity markets on acceptable terms the binding condition on the growth plan. The liquidity set out in the balance sheet section covers the near term; it does not fund the full plan.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
Atmos Energy trades at 18.7x trailing earnings and an EV/EBITDA of 14.0x, a multiple that, unlike P/E, counts the company's net debt, which stood at $8.7B at FY25 year-end. Fiscal 2026 ended September 30, 2026, so FY27E is now the next twelve months, and on FY27E consensus EPS of $9.02 the shares trade at ~17.4x. The vendor's 18.6x forward (NTM) figure sits next to the trailing multiple and well above that FY27E multiple, so we read it as resting on earnings near the FY26E level of $8.46 and use the FY27E multiple as the forward multiple. Price-to-sales of 5.4x says little here, because revenue includes passed-through gas costs. The dividend yield is 2.56%.

Peer multiples are not available on this page, so we judge value against the Street, the stock's own trading range and our scenarios. The consensus target is $185.00 (+17.8%), the median target $183.00 and the range $167.00–$206.00, so every Street target sits above the current price. The shares traded as high as $192.51 over the past 52 weeks and now sit just above the $154.72 low. No source on the page explains the fall, and the latest company document on the page, the August 5, 2026 earnings release, reaffirmed guidance. The Street's targets come with 12 Hold ratings out of 14, so we do not read the targets alone as a reason to expect a recovery. Without peer or historical multiples on the page we do not call the stock cheap or expensive.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Regulators approve most of the $373.4 million of ratemaking requests in progress, FY27 EPS meets or beats consensus, and the shares re-rate above today's trailing multiple toward where they traded before the fall. We price it at the $185.00 consensus target, below the $192.51 52-week high.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Fiscal 2026 lands within the $8.40 - $8.50 guidance and FY27E consensus EPS of $9.02 is met. A year out those become trailing earnings, and we hold today's 18.7x trailing multiple on them, which gives about $169: the shares earn one year of consensus growth and neither win back nor extend the fall from the 52-week high.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The Texas infrastructure-legislation benefit ends, regulators disallow part of the pending requests and equity is issued at lower prices, so FY27 earnings fall back to the FY25 level of $7.46 per diluted share. On those trailing earnings the shares carry the ~17.4x they trade at on FY27E today, below the Base's multiple, which gives about $130.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
All three cases price FY27 earnings a year out on a trailing multiple: above today's trailing multiple in the Bull, today's trailing multiple in the Base and the lower FY27E forward multiple in the Bear. We weight the Base at 60% and the Bull and Bear at 20% each. The Bull needs a re-rating that no source on the page points to, while most covering analysts rate the shares Hold. The Bear needs several things to go wrong at once. Implemented rate outcomes of $355.0 million and weather normalization on approximately 97 percent of residential and commercial revenues argue against a full reset. Still, the 10-Q does not say whether the Texas benefit persists, so the Bear is a real outcome rather than a remote one.

The weighted fair value is $164.40, an expected upside of +4.7% against a Bear-case downside of 17.2%, a reward/risk of 0.27×. That falls short of both BUY bars, and it is the basis of our HOLD.

The Base anchor decides how close the call is. Holding today's forward multiple on FY27E instead would return about today's price and leave expected upside near zero, still HOLD. Anchoring the Base to the median Street target would just reach BUY at these weights. In favor of that anchor, every Street target sits above the price, guidance was reaffirmed, and nothing on the page shows the fundamentals weakening as the shares fell. Against it, the same analysts mostly rate the shares Hold, and assuming the market reverses a fall no source explains is a forecast of sentiment, not of earnings. We hold the trailing multiple, which credits a year of consensus growth without assuming a recovery. That is a judgment, and it is what separates our HOLD from a BUY.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The third-party revenue series carries Atmos Energy as a single consolidated revenue line, while the 10-Q manages the business as two reportable segments, distribution and pipeline and storage; we use the consolidated line for revenue and the 10-Q for segment commentary. Distribution carries most of the revenue: its operating revenues were $774,658 thousand in the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Approximately 70 percent of distribution revenues are earned in the six months through March, so the June quarter is seasonally light. Pipeline and storage centers on Atmos Pipeline-Texas, which transports natural gas for third parties and manages five underground storage facilities in Texas.

moatFactors.name: Regulated distribution franchise
moatFactors.body: The company is the regulated gas distributor in over 1,400 communities across its service areas, with a network of more than 81,000 miles of distribution and transmission lines. Duplicating that network is not economic for a new entrant; the competitive threat the company itself lists is competition from energy suppliers and alternative forms of energy.

moatFactors.name: Lag-reducing rate design
moatFactors.body: Approximately 50 percent of distribution revenue, excluding gas costs, is recovered through the base customer charge. Weather normalization adjustments cover approximately 97 percent of residential and commercial revenues, and rate design lets the company collect the gas cost portion of bad debt expense on approximately 89 percent of residential and commercial revenues. In our view this design protects margin well against weather swings and gas-price-driven bad debt, which is what makes it strong. Its limit is volume: the rest of non-gas distribution revenue still depends on usage, and most weather normalization windows close in the spring, so the protection is strong rather than complete.

moatFactors.name: Texas pipeline and storage assets
moatFactors.body: The pipeline and storage segment owns 5,700 miles of gas transmission lines and provides ancillary services such as parking arrangements, lending and inventory sales. These assets give the company its own transmission and storage capacity, though their returns are also regulated.

businessMoat.durability:
The franchise itself is durable. Much of the capital program earns recovery through the lag-reducing mechanisms discussed in the financials section, and most of it is safety and reliability work that the company says it is accelerating with the support from each of its regulatory commissions.

We rate the moat NARROW rather than WIDE for two reasons, both set out in the risks section: returns are set by regulators, and the company itself says full recovery of its planned spending is not assured; and natural gas faces long-run policy risk to its volumes.

points: The company anticipates spending approximately $26 billion between fiscal years 2026 and 2030, with more than 80 percent dedicated to safety and reliability. That spending becomes rate base, the main driver of earnings for a regulated utility.
Ratemaking actions implemented during the nine months ended June 30, 2026 raised annual operating income by $355.0 million, and efforts in progress at that date sought a further $373.4 million.
Division gains are concentrated in Mid-Tex, where the MD&A places most of the quarter's rate adjustments and customer growth; we read that concentration as a risk in the risks section.

Consensus FY26E EPS of $8.46 sits inside the reaffirmed $8.40 - $8.50 guidance, so the Street already assumes the guidance is met and fiscal 2026 holds little surprise either way; the FY27E figure of $9.02 depends on the ratemaking requests in progress converting into outcomes.

Comparisons get tougher from here, and this is our inference rather than the company's: the Texas infrastructure legislation took effect during the third quarter of fiscal 2025, so year-over-year comparisons will increasingly include its benefit on both sides. The 10-Q does not say whether that benefit persists, grows or ends, so we expect it to add less to year-over-year growth without assuming it disappears.

management.leadership: J. Kevin Akers is President and Chief Executive Officer, according to the December 2025 proxy statement. The company frames its strategy around a vision to be the safest provider of natural gas services, which ties capital spending to the safety rules regulators reward. The proxy sections reviewed here do not give tenure or biographies, so we judge the team on results: the rate outcomes and capital deployment set out in the growth section read to us as competent execution of a plan regulators have so far supported.
management.capitalAllocation:
Capital goes overwhelmingly to the network: over 85 percent of nine-month capital expenditures went to improving the safety and reliability of the distribution and transportation systems. The cash flow series carries no share repurchase data for FY21 to FY25, so the shareholder returns on the surface come through dividends.

The Board declared a quarterly dividend of $1.00 per share, and the indicated annual dividend for fiscal 2026 is $4.00, a {+ 14.9% +} increase over fiscal 2025. We read a raise of that size, made while the company relies on outside capital, as a signal of management's confidence in the rate-outcome path rather than as evidence of surplus cash. The use of equity forward sales agreements suggests management is pacing dilution deliberately.
management.governance:
The December 2025 proxy statement reports that, for fiscal 2025, the Board determined every director other than Mr. Akers to be independent under NYSE and SEC rules; Mr. Akers is not independent because he is the Company's President and Chief Executive Officer. The Board runs an annual self-evaluation through written questionnaires for the Board and each committee, and related party transactions above $100,000 in which a related person has a material interest go to the Governance Committee for review and approval.

For shareholders, a board that is independent apart from the CEO, with a formal review of related party dealings, is a sound structure, and we see no governance flag in the excerpt. The proxy sections reviewed here do not cover executive compensation, so we make no judgment on pay.
management.insiderOwnership:
As of December 12, 2025, Mr. Akers beneficially owned 173,855 shares, per the proxy statement. The excerpt does not give his percent of class, so we do not size the stake against the ~168.99M shares outstanding; we read it as a real personal exposure to the share price, and so a meaningful alignment signal, without treating it as influence over the company.

The same proxy lists The Vanguard Group, Inc. at 12.0%, BlackRock, Inc. at 7.9%, State Street Corporation at 6.9%, Capital International Investors at 6.5% and Wellington Management Group LLP and certain affiliates at 6.5%. No holder controls the company and every holder listed is an asset manager, so governance outcomes rest on the independent board rather than on any single owner. Several of those positions rest on Schedule 13G filings for the period ending December 31, 2023, so they are dated, and none reflects trading since December 2025.

idiosyncratic: **Regulatory recovery.** Regulators monitor returns continuously and can limit or disallow costs or modify or terminate the infrastructure and annual rate mechanisms that cut lag. A change there would hit earnings directly, since the capital plan assumes timely recovery.

**Texas concentration.** The 10-Q lists the concentration of operations in Texas as a risk, and the quarter shows it: Mid-Tex operating income rose to $74,313 thousand from $48,244 thousand, more than the distribution segment's total increase. Elsewhere, Mississippi operating income fell to $1,803 thousand from $6,967 thousand and Louisiana to $13,760 thousand from $18,747 thousand, so a Texas regulatory or legislative change would move the whole segment.

**Operational safety.** Leaks, explosions or fire near populated areas could bring liability, fines and repair costs beyond insurance limits and deductibles, and would damage the regulatory goodwill the rate mechanisms depend on.

**Funding.** If the market access we treat as the binding condition in the financials section tightens, or the share price falls too far to issue equity efficiently, the company would have to slow the plan or accept more dilution.
risks.systemic:
Interest rates pressure utility valuations as bond yields compete with the dividend, and they set the cost of the funding gap described in the financials section. Natural gas prices pass through to customers, but higher gas costs can raise bad debt and short-term borrowing and push customers to conserve.

Longer term, the company lists legislation to reduce or eliminate greenhouse gas emissions or fossil fuels and the impact of climate change among its risks; both threaten volumes and political support for gas infrastructure. Adverse weather and economic conditions in the service areas complete the macro exposure, though weather normalization blunts the weather effect.

body: We rate Atmos Energy **HOLD** with a target range of $150–$185. The regulated growth engine is working, and leverage is moderate for a utility. What holds us back is the valuation set out above: without a re-rating, the shares offer about a year of consensus growth against a Bear case that is a real outcome. The page's advisory distress gate does not set this label.

We would move to BUY on approval of the pending ratemaking requests without a material disallowance together with evidence that FY27 earnings are running ahead of the $9.02 consensus, or on a fall in the price just under the low end of our target range with fundamentals intact, which is where our scenarios reach the BUY line. We would move to SELL if a ruling or legislative change ended the Texas benefit, or if the shares rallied past the $167.00 lowest Street target without higher earnings expectations, since our scenarios derive SELL before the price reaches the $183.00 median.
